p21: 21.  In a judgment of 19 November 2008 the District Court granted T.’s request and ordered the child’s immediate return to Australia, no later than six weeks from the date of its decision. In its reasoning, noting that the Australian authorities had established that the applicant and T. had joint parental responsibility, the court first considered that the Latvian courts could neither revisit that decision nor interpret and apply Australian law. It further held that, under Articles 1 and 14 of the Hague Convention, the Latvian courts did not have jurisdiction to rule on T.’s parental responsibility in respect of the child, but only on the child’s departure from Australia and her possible return. It found that the child’s removal had been wrongful and had taken place without T.’s consent. As to the application of Article 13 of the Hague Convention, it considered, in the light of photographs and copies of e-mails exchanged between the applicant and T.’s relatives, that the latter had taken care of the child before her departure for Latvia. While noting that witness statements referred to quarrels between the parents and to the fact that T. had allegedly behaved irascibly towards the applicant and the child, it held that this did not warrant the assertion that T. had not taken care of the child. Lastly, the court dismissed the allegation of a risk of psychological harm to the child in the event of her return, finding it to be merely an unsubstantiated assumption.
p22: 22.  The applicant appealed, submitting that on the date of their departure from Australia she had been the child’s sole de jure and de facto guardian and, furthermore, that her daughter’s return to Australia would expose her to psychological harm. On the latter point she produced a certificate drawn up at her request by a psychologist after the first-instance judgment. p23: 23.  The applicant also argued on appeal that Latvian was the child’s mother tongue, that she had attended pre-school activities in Latvia, that she had no ties in Australia and that she needed her mother’s presence. She alleged that T. had never helped them financially and had ill-treated them. Furthermore, she criticised the first-instance judge for refusing to ask the Australian authorities for information about T.’s criminal profile, his previous convictions and the charges of bribery which, according to her, had been brought against him. She further asserted that if she returned to Australia she would be without employment or resources, and criticised the District Court for failing to provide for protective measures in the event of a return.
p24: 24.  On 6 January 2009, on an application by the applicant, the District Court stayed the enforcement of the return order of 19 November 2008 pending the examination of the appeal. Relying on the preamble to the Hague Convention, it held that the child’s interests had to take precedence over her immediate return, that the child was attached to her mother and that, according to the psychological report submitted by the latter, an abrupt interruption of contact with her mother would traumatise her.
p25: 25.  On 26 January 2009, following a hearing in the presence of the applicant and T., the Rīga Regional Court (*Rīgas Apgabaltiesa*) upheld the first-instance judgment. It held that T.’s request was in conformity with the Hague Convention, while reiterating the short time-limits laid down therein and observing that no formalities or analysis were necessary in order to recognise the decision of the Australian court. It further considered that the lower court had correctly established, on the basis of all the relevant evidence, in particular the letters and photographs produced, that T. had taken care of the child.
